messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night the cables snapped, Elias Vance was still in command on his set. It was a coastal shoot, and the production had pushed past dusk to catch the fading light. When the rig failed, the sudden metallic shriek tore through the air before the lighting tower collapsed onto his left leg. He remembered the impact as a series of frozen frames: the way the steel beam crushed his ankle, the red spread across his trousers, and the emergency generator failing, plunging the set into absolute blackness. He could not articulate what happened in those first few minutes; his mind refused to form sentences, leaving only the raw, untranslatable images of metal and blood pressed into his awareness. As the weeks unfolded, those unblinking pictures began to dictate his days. He could not shake the detailed frames of the collapsed rig, and they quietly shifted how he viewed his own competence. He had come to believe he was fundamentally inadequate, that surviving the accident while others bled nearby proved he had failed to protect himself. What frightened him most was not the event itself, but the way those unprocessed images constantly primed his nervous system for danger. His body braced before his mind could catch up, and ordinary drops—camera cases, steering wheels, even his partner’s keys on the kitchen counter—snatched his breath and sent him jolting backward. He tried to make sense of why the event has happened to him, and he distracts himself with something else whenever the dread rises, telling himself that if he just stays occupied, he will not unravel. The effort to distract himself from the sudden jolts only leaves him exhausted by late afternoon. His inability to trust his own reactions soon dictated his behavior. Feeling certain he was a lousy coper, he began steering clear of any environment where visibility faltered, and he deliberately packed his schedule to avoid the quiet moments where his thoughts might drift. He could not sit in a dimly lit office, and he could not endure the sudden jolt of a slamming door, so he demanded bright workspaces and preemptively excused himself from crowded rooms. The avoidance grew into a rigid routine that began to fracture his professional standing. His crew grew frustrated with the excessive lighting rigs he insisted upon, and the delays caused him to lose the confidence he once commanded on set. His partner stopped waiting for him to come home, noting that he had become a watchful stranger who flinched at every shift in the room. Over the following months, the habit of retreating from the dark and forcing himself into distraction only tightened the grip on his own experience. Each time he fled an unlit hallway or buried his attention in a screen, the avoided moments festered, making the visual fragments of the accident flash with greater intensity the moment he stopped moving. That renewed intrusion of images left him feeling wholly inadequate, and the conviction that he had become unrecognizable to himself amplified the sense of imminent danger until every ordinary noise demanded his full attention. The more he distrusted his own coping, the more he monitored his surroundings for threats, and the more his body remained locked in a state of perpetual watchfulness. He recognized that his attempts to shield himself from darkness and sound were only feeding the very reactions he dreaded, creating a rhythm of panic and retreat that no longer allowed him to think clearly. It was the silence of his own apartment that finally broke his resolve. His partner had left a note on the counter after another missed dinner, and the realization that he was disappearing from his own life forced him to the door. He sat in the intake room now, hoping someone could help him quiet the relentless scanning and stop feeling like a stranger to his own history. He was terrified of returning to the set, but he desperately wanted to stop waiting for the next collapse.
